name: Sam Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck at the copper pit, a big yellow thing that carries about two hundred and twenty tonnes a load. Shift starts at six with a prestart meeting, then I walk round my truck, check the tyres, the lights, the fluids, and I'm out on the ramp by half past. All day it's load at the shovel, down to the crusher, tip, back up again, maybe forty loads if the shovel's running sweet. I like the quiet in the cab and I like the guys on the radio, but twelve hours of that ramp on nights wears you down in a way my wife says she can see in my face.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who are the guys on the radio? Who do you spend the day with?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Dev on the shovel, he's been loading me for nine years and we can talk a whole shift in about ten words. There's Marta in dispatch who knows everyone's kids' names. At crib time, that's our lunch break, we sit in the same hut and argue about football and the union deal. Over in the north pit they've already got driverless trucks on trial, six of them, and nobody in our hut talks about that for long, you just sort of change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I told you so. Every year someone comes into the prestart with a new slide about the future and it mostly ends up as another form on a tablet. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd say it at the barbecue, AI was a lot of noise and the work still needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI hype was never the thing that scared me. It's the trucks in the north pit, and those were coming whether the chatbots got clever or not. So even in this picture I'm not totally relaxed, I'm just not worse off than I am today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, keep my head down, keep paying my union dues. I'd want the union to push hard in the next agreement for a rule that nobody loses their job when a truck goes driverless, because the plateau doesn't stop that. Other than that, nothing changes, the mortgage still comes out on the fifteenth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with that same little knot I already carry. It's the knot you get when you drive past the north pit and see a truck with nobody in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the north pit trucks were coming anyway. What happens to the drivers there now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of them got moved to our pit or to the water carts, so far nobody's been sacked. But there's no new starters in the north, and that's how they do it, they don't fire you, they just don't hire the next one. My cousin's boy applied twice and never heard back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their dad's job is fine for now and to eat their vegetables. Mateo's eleven and he thinks the driverless trucks are cool, he watched a video of them. I didn't have the heart to tell him what I think of that video.

S0.say: I'd tell everyone at work and at the barbecue that AI was mostly noise and that the pit still needs people. I'd say it with a bit of told-you-so in my voice.
S0.think: The AI hype was never my real worry, the driverless trucks in the north pit are. They were coming anyway, so I'm not relaxed, I'm just no worse off than today.
S0.do: Keeps driving and keeps paying union dues. Wants the union to push for a no-job-loss rule on driverless trucks in the next agreement, and otherwise changes nothing.
S0.feel: Relief, with the same quiet knot he already carries when he passes the north pit.
S0.quote: They don't fire you, they just don't hire the next one.
S0.fieldNote: Sam separates AI hype from the robots he can already see from his cab, and he's far more worried about the second. Even in the calmest picture he carries a background worry. His instinct is to hand the problem to the union rather than act on his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, the company will use this to cut heads and call it safety. I'd say it in the hut and I'd say it at the union meeting. If the work changes, fine, but the people who've done it for twenty years should get first dibs on whatever the new jobs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think trucks like mine are first on the list. Driving loaded down a ramp is about the most repeatable job on the whole site, and that's me. I'm forty-three, I've got a trade certificate and a truck licence, and I'm not a computer person, so if the new jobs are in a control room I'm not sure they'd pick me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting, which I don't do now, maybe one in three. I'd want us to fight for retraining paid by the company and for redundancy at four weeks per year instead of two. At home we'd stop the second car loan we were thinking about and try to get the savings from about three months up to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. It's not panic, it's more like the feeling before a big storm when you're checking the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the new jobs might be in a control room. Would you try for one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I suppose. My mate Joel did a week on the remote panel for the trial trucks and he said it's like watching six tellies at once. I don't want to sit in an air-conditioned box babysitting machines, I want to drive. But I know wanting doesn't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camping trip at Easter, that's about eight hundred dollars once you add fuel. Then the kids' footy fees would stay but the new boots wouldn't. My wife Lucia drives a school bus, so her money's steady, and that's what we'd lean on.

S1.say: I'd say the company will use AI to cut heads and call it safety. The people who've done the work for twenty years should get first pick of any new jobs.
S1.think: Driving loaded down a ramp is about the most repeatable job on site, so I'm first on the list. I'm not a computer person and I'm not sure they'd pick me for a control room job.
S1.do: Goes to every union meeting and pushes for company-paid retraining and better redundancy. Drops a planned second car loan and tries to grow savings from about three months to six.
S1.feel: A tight chest, like checking the windows before a storm.
S1.quote: I don't want to sit in an air-conditioned box babysitting machines, I want to drive.
S1.fieldNote: Sam's public line and private fear line up: he blames the company openly and privately thinks his own job is the easiest to replace. He'd fight collectively but resists retraining himself. Lucia's school bus income is his quiet safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disgrace and the government has to step in, today, not next year. I'd be one of the ones posting it, honestly, which I never do. Somebody has to say that a mine making billions doesn't get to throw a whole town out in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it means for me is I'm gone. Not maybe, gone, because a robot that can drive and fix and load is everything I do. Two years is nothing, our mortgage has eighteen left on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't food, power and the mortgage. I'd go to the union and say we need to be on the street, at the gate, at the member of parliament's office. I'd ring my brother in the city about whether we could stay with him if it came to that, and I'd look into what the government would pay us, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor's been taken out. I keep thinking about Mateo and that video he loves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do differently than if you had more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no plan, there's only holding on. If you gave me ten years I could at least watch it come and sell the house before everyone else does. With two, the whole town's trying to sell at the same time and you get nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on government help. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, actually, that's what it's for, I've paid tax every week since I was eighteen. What scares me is that it won't be there, or that it'll be some form you have to fill in on a website. I don't do websites. Lucia does all that and she'll be just as scared as me.

S2.say: I'd call it a disgrace and say the government has to step in now. I'd even post about it, which I never do, because a mine making billions shouldn't be allowed to throw out a town in two years.
S2.think: I'm gone, not maybe. A robot that can drive and fix and load is everything I do, and two years is nothing against an eighteen-year mortgage.
S2.do: Stops all spending beyond food, power and the mortgage in the first month. Pushes the union to protest at the gate and at the local MP's office, asks his brother about moving in, and looks up government support for the first time.
S2.feel: Sick, like the floor has gone. He keeps thinking about his son.
S2.quote: With two years there's no plan, there's only holding on.
S2.fieldNote: Sam moves straight to collective protest and public support, which fits his politics, but he's frightened the help won't reach someone who doesn't "do websites". He sees the fast timeline as a crowd problem: everyone selling houses at once. This is the only picture where he says he'd post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them to make the companies pay. Tax the robots, put the money into the towns. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it to anyone who'd stand still long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of room, but I'm still the one being replaced. I'm not going to turn into a programmer at forty-five. What I really think is my job's got maybe three good years and then I'm on whatever the government sets up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the savings to six months as fast as I could, which means no holidays, nothing. I'd get on the union committee, actually stand for it, and work on a deal that pays out drivers properly. I'd tell Lucia we should pay extra on the mortgage while I still have overtime, maybe two hundred a fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but with something to do with it. That's better than the fast one, where I'd just be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stand for the union committee. What would you fight for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three things. Full pay for two years for anyone the robots replace, a seat at the table when they decide which pit goes first, and the company paying for the kids of miners to get trained in whatever's next. The last one's the one I care about, if I'm finished, at least Rosa shouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can pay down a bit and maybe not lose the house. It doesn't change that I'm not going to be a different person. My mate Joel would take a course, good luck to him, but I'd rather use my time fighting for a fair deal than sitting in a classroom I'd fail.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so let's make the companies pay. Tax the robots and put the money back into the mining towns.
S3.think: Five years is a bit of room but I'm still the one being replaced. My job has maybe three good years left and then I'm on whatever the government sets up.
S3.do: Pushes savings toward six months by cutting holidays and pays about two hundred extra a fortnight on the mortgage while overtime lasts. Stands for the union committee to fight for full pay for replaced drivers and training for miners' children.
S3.feel: Scared, but with something to do with the fear, which feels better than the fast picture.
S3.quote: If I'm finished, at least Rosa shouldn't be.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time turns Sam's panic into organising, not personal change. He openly rules out retraining and puts his energy into a deal for others and for his kids. He'd move from sometimes-member to committee candidate, a real step for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse not to. Every government that's in during those ten years should be judged on what they set up for workers. I'd say that at the union and at the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably be fifty-three when it lands, and that's a terrible age, too young to stop, too old to start. The ten years helps the kids a lot more than it helps me. I'd keep driving as long as there's a truck with a seat in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and pay the mortgage down hard, maybe a few hundred extra a month, so it's nearly gone by the time the robots are. I'd push the union for an early-retirement deal for people over fifty. And I'd sit down with Mateo and Rosa and steer them off mining, which hurts to say, because my dad was a fitter at this same mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not like the fast one. It's more grief than fear, like watching your old dog get slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years helps the kids more than you. What would you tell Mateo when he picks his subjects?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to pick something where people want a person, nursing like his aunty, or teaching. Not mining, not trucking. He'd argue with me because he loves the big machines, and I'd lose, probably, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd rather fight than sit in a classroom. With ten years, would you change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd do my loader ticket, that's a few days, not a classroom really. But I'm not kidding myself, a loader's a machine too and it'll go the same way. I'd rather spend the ten years making sure there's a pension worth having when they let me go.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse. I'd judge every government in that decade on what it sets up for workers.
S4.think: I'd be about fifty-three when it lands, too young to stop and too old to start. The ten years helps my kids more than me, so I'd keep driving while there's a seat.
S4.do: Keeps driving and pays a few hundred extra a month on the mortgage so it's nearly gone in time. Pushes for an early-retirement deal for over-fifties and steers his children away from mining.
S4.feel: Heavy, more grief than fear, like watching an old dog get slow.
S4.quote: I'd probably be fifty-three when it lands, and that's a terrible age, too young to stop, too old to start.
S4.fieldNote: Even with a decade Sam stays alarmed, because the extra time doesn't change his own reluctance to learn something new. His focus shifts to his children and a pension, and his politics come through in judging governments by what they do for workers. The family history at the mine makes steering his kids away painful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is real money, paid automatically, not something you apply for on a website, and a union strong enough that the company can't just switch us off. Also someone from the government actually coming to our town and talking to us in the hall, not on the news.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the families. When a pit shuts it's not just the drivers, it's the bakery, the school bus, the footy club. Lucia's job goes too if the families leave. People think of us one at a time but a mining town falls over all at once.

headlineQuote: A mining town falls over all at once.
portrait: Sam Garcia is a 43-year-old haul truck driver at a large copper pit, with a partner who drives a school bus, two kids and eighteen years left on the mortgage. He loves driving and dislikes screens, and he already watches driverless trucks on trial in the next pit. Through the five pictures he turns again and again to the union and to government, and he openly rules out retraining himself. His mood climbs from uneasy to panicked in the two-year picture, and extra warning time mainly helps him protect the house and steer his kids away from mining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because with two years there's no plan, only holding on, and the whole town would be selling up at once.
whatWouldHelp: Real money paid automatically rather than through a website, a strong union, and government people coming to talk to the town in person.
